1.evidence_source: Factor structure and psychometric properties of the Body Appreciation Scale-2 among adolescents and young adults in Danish, Portuguese, and Swedish
1._section_summary: This section presents the title and author line of a paper examining the factor structure and psychometric properties of the Body Appreciation Scale-2 among adolescents and young adults in Danish, Portuguese, and Swedish. The title indicates the BAS-2 instrument was used and that samples span Danish, Portuguese, and Swedish contexts; no explicit study numbers, sample sizes, methods, or statistics are provided in the text excerpt.

2.evidence_source: The present study seeks to validate a measure of positive body image, the Body Appreciation Scale-2 (BAS-2; Tylka & Wood-Barcalow, 2015a) in Denmark, Portugal, and Sweden.
2._section_summary: This abstract reports a single cross-national validation of the Body Appreciation Scale-2 (BAS-2) in Denmark, Portugal, and Sweden with N = 1012 adolescents and young adults (ages 12–19). Confirmatory factor analyses supported a one-factor structure and invariance across sex and country; BAS-2 correlated positively with self-esteem, psychological well-being, and intuitive eating, and showed negative correlations with BMI for both boys and girls in Portugal but not in Denmark and Sweden. The abstract does not report survey method, racial composition, mean age, mean BMI, or whether BMI was self-reported or measured.

3.evidence_source: The present study aimed to validate the BAS-2 among adolescents and young adults from three different countries: Denmark, Portugal, and Sweden.
3._section_summary: This Introduction reviews the development of the Body Appreciation Scale and its 10-item revision (BAS-2), summarizes prior cross-cultural validations, and motivates validating the BAS-2 in Denmark, Portugal, and Sweden. The present study (singular) aims to examine the BAS-2 factor structure, measurement invariance across sex and country, and convergent validity (including correlations with self-esteem, well-being, intuitive eating, and BMI) among adolescent and young adult males and females in these three countries.

4.evidence_source: The total sample consisted of 1012 adolescents and young adults (482 boys and 530 girls)from Denmark (n = 129), Portugal(n = 513), and Sweden (n = 370).
4._section_summary: This section describes a single study sample of 1012 adolescents and young adults (482 boys, 530 girls) from Denmark (n = 129), Portugal (n = 513), and Sweden (n = 370). Participants were aged 12–19 (overall M = 15.1, SD = 1.9; country means reported) and self-reported BMI (range 11.72–51.14; overall M = 21.01; country means reported). The section does not report survey method, participant ethnicity, recruitment/source, assessment of body appreciation (BAS/BAS-2), or correlations between body appreciation and BMI.

5.evidence_source: "The questionnaires which were not available in Danish, Portuguese, and Swedish were translated in the respective languages..."; "Two boys and two girls from 12 to 19 years old were recruited by country."
5._section_summary: This Measures section describes translation of questionnaires into Danish, Portuguese, and Swedish using back-translation and pilot testing in the target audiences. Pilot testing involved two boys and two girls (aged 12–19) recruited by country who were interviewed to assess item clarity; participants reported BAS-2 items were clear. No study numbering (e.g., 'Study 1') or statistical results (e.g., BMI, correlations) are reported in this section.

6.evidence_source: The already validated Portuguese version (Pechorro, Marôco, Poiares, & Vieira, 2011) was used in Portugal.

It cites prior psychometric properties (Cronbach's α and 1-week stability) from other studies but provides no details about the current study's sample size, demographics, BMI, survey method, body appreciation measures, or correlations.

7.evidence_source: The study was approved by the ethics committee of the National Committee on Health Research Ethics in Denmark (number H-16044295), the Ethics Committee of the Faculty of Psychology and Education Sciences of the University of Porto in Portugal(reference 6-05/2016), and the Ethical Committee at Lund University in Sweden (number 2016/264).
7._section_summary: This procedures section states that passive parental consent and active participant consent were obtained and that participants completed an online questionnaire at school during class with counterbalanced scale order; demographics were collected. It also lists ethics approvals obtained in Denmark, Portugal, and Sweden. The section does not label the study (no 'Study 1' or multiple studies are mentioned) and does not provide sample size, age, BMI, assessment instruments, or demographic breakdowns.

Sample sizes are given (N = 1012; country- and gender-specific ns: 79 Danish girls, 50 Danish boys, 296 Portuguese girls, 217 Portuguese boys, 155 Swedish girls, 215 Swedish boys), and item loadings are described (Item 5 lowest, .44–.70; most loadings > .60). The section does not report survey method, demographics (age, race), BMI means, BA/BMI correlations, or assessment instruments in the provided text.

Sample sizes are reported (N = 1012; Danish girls n = 79, Danish boys n = 50, Portuguese girls n = 296, Portuguese boys n = 217, Swedish girls n = 155, Swedish boys n = 215), and most item loadings were > .60 with Item 5 the lowest (.44 to .70) but retained.

12._section_summary: This section reports confirmatory factor analyses (CFAs) of the BAS-2 conducted across three countries (Denmark, Portugal, Sweden) for both boys and girls. All indicators loaded significantly on a unidimensional factor (mostly p < .001), with Item 5 showing the lowest loadings and Item 8 having p = .002 in the Danish boy sample. The results and factor loadings are presented in Tables 2 and 3 (Table 3 shows standardized item-factor loadings by country and gender; total N = 1012).

13.evidence_source: The results displayed in Table 4 and Supplementary Table 5 indicate that there was evidence of metric and partial scalar invariance across Denmark and Portugal (metric -CFI = .003, scalar -CFI = .024, and partial scalar -CFI = .008); Denmark and Sweden (metric -CFI = .001, scalar -CFI = .016, and partial scalar -CFI = .008); and Portugal and Sweden (metric -CFI = .004, scalar -CFI = .020, and partial scalar -CFI = .007).
13._section_summary: This section reports multi-group confirmatory factor analyses testing measurement invariance of the BAS-2 across Denmark, Portugal, and Sweden and across boys and girls. Results (reported in Table 4 and Supplementary Table 5) indicate evidence of metric and partial scalar invariance across the country pairs and metric and (partial) scalar invariance across sexes within the three countries.

14.evidence_source: Scores on the Danish, Portuguese, and Swedish versions of the BAS-2 were shown to be internally consistentfor both boys ( = .92, .91, and .94, respectively) and girls ( = .93, .94, and .94, respectively).
14._section_summary: This section reports internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha) for the Danish, Portuguese, and Swedish versions of the BAS-2, with separate alpha values provided for boys and girls. No other sample details (e.g., sample size, age, BMI, survey method) or correlations with BMI are reported in this excerpt. The section does not label any study as 'Study 1' or similar.

15.evidence_source: “Convergent validity was assessed by looking at the correlations between the BAS-2 and self-esteem, psychological well-being, intuitive eating, and BMI for boys and girls in Denmark, Portugal, and Sweden separately.”
15._section_summary: This section reports convergent validity analyses of the BAS-2 across adolescent samples in Denmark, Portugal, and Sweden, examining correlations with self-esteem, psychological well-being, intuitive eating, and BMI separately for boys and girls. For girls a weak relationship between BAS-2 and BMI is described and reported as significant only in Portugal (r = .14, p = .015) but not in Denmark or Sweden; for boys a weak negative relationship was found in Portugal (r = −.33, p < .001) but not in the other countries. The section references Tables 5–7 and Supplementary Tables 3 and 4 and notes generally similar patterns across countries.

16.evidence_source: Results showed that the level of body appreciation was not significantly different across the three countries: Denmark (M = 3.89, SD = 0.78), Portugal (M = 4.01, SD = 0.79), and Sweden (M = 3.89, SD = 0.90).
16.warning: Sentence describing country means is fragmented in the source text.
16._section_summary: A two-way ANOVA tested body appreciation by sex and country: there was a significant main effect of sex (F(1, 1006) = 105.45, p < .001), with boys (M = 4.21, SD = 0.73) reporting higher body appreciation than girls (M = 3.72, SD = 0.85). There was a small but significant main effect of country (F(2, 1006) = 3.42, p = .033), with reported means for Denmark (M = 3.89, SD = 0.78), Portugal (M = 4.01, SD = 0.79), and Sweden (M = 3.89, SD = 0.90); the sex-by-country interaction was non-significant (F(2, 1006) = 0.75, p = .475). The section also includes notes indicating multiple subgroup sample sizes for correlation matrices (e.g., girl n = 79 and boy n = 50; girl n = 296 and boy n = 217; girl n = 155 and boy n = 215).

21.evidence_source: The main objective of the study was to accrue psychometric evidence for the BAS-2 among adolescents and young adults in three countries: Denmark, Portugal, and Sweden.
21._section_summary: This Discussion reports psychometric support for the BAS-2 across adolescent samples from Denmark, Portugal, and Sweden, finding a single-factor structure and partial scalar invariance across countries and sexes. The BAS-2 showed positive convergent validity with self-esteem, psychological well-being, and intuitive eating, and relationships with BMI differed by country (negative in Portugal; nonsignificant in Denmark and Sweden). The authors note limitations including school-based recruitment (few schools per country) and absence of full adult samples.
